title: I Adopted ZEN: The First Week
excerpt: ZEN came home on September 28 — sleeping, eating, and being hissed at. Notes from the first seven days.
content:
Introduction: ZEN, A Very Small Cat

　A kitten named ZEN came home with me on September 28. Smaller than I expected — small enough that one hand covers most of the head, and light enough that I was not sure I was actually holding anything. I had read about cats for years, but nothing prepares you for the first time a living creature closes its eyes and simply trusts you with the whole of itself.


Why ZEN

　The name was already printed on the card at the shelter, and I almost changed it. A friend pointed out that ZEN is the same word as 禅 — stillness, the quiet that arrives once the mind finally stops arguing with itself. I kept it on the card, and then I kept it for real. Cats are mostly stillness with one short violent interval in between, and ZEN sits firmly on the quiet side of that ratio.


1. The First Night: Crying in the Box

　The first night, ZEN cried almost continuously. The advice I had been given was simple: prepare one quiet room with food, water, and a litter box, and keep the door closed. Cats are small; a big house is confusing when everything is new. The crying is not a demand to be let out — it is the process of accepting that this is now home. By the second night the voice had dropped to a faint complaint. By the third it had stopped.


2. Food and Water: The Slow Phase

　Kittens have small stomachs and fast metabolisms, so they need several small meals a day rather than one large bowl. Wet food works well at this age because it contains enough water, which matters while ZEN is still learning to drink from a bowl. A kitten that seems to hesitate often prefers food that has been warmed slightly — room temperature or lukewarm — because cold food straight from the fridge is closer in temperature to the outside world than to a body.


3. The Litter Box Lesson

　This part was almost unnervingly easy. I placed the box where ZEN had already been sniffing the floor, kept it uncovered, and kept it clean. Cats bury their own waste instinctively, so the main job of a human is simply to keep the location stable and the litter clean. A single accident outside the box is not a failure of training; it usually means the box is too far away, too small, or too dirty.


4. Play Is Training

　Two short play sessions a day, using a wand toy or a ball rather than fingers, make a surprising difference. Kittens are born with a prey instinct that has not yet learned where it ends. Playing teaches the rhythm of the hunt — stalk, pounce, capture — and also teaches the limit: a hand that moves is a toy, a hand that stops is something to be left alone. This is not entertainment. It is the single best thing an owner can teach in the first month, and ZEN learned it faster than I expected.


5. The First Vet Visit

　The first visit is worth doing early rather than waiting. It covers deworming, a check for fleas and ear mites, and the start of the vaccination schedule, with follow-up shots given at intervals rather than all at once. A kitten should gain weight steadily, and asking for the exact number at each visit — rather than a vague impression of small but healthy — is the easiest way to catch a problem early.


6. The First Week in Practice

　By the end of the week the routine had settled into something ordinary: wake, feed, play, clean the box, feed again, sleep on the desk where a keyboard should be. What surprised me most was the rhythm of it. A cat is not a pet in the sense of a decoration that responds on demand; it is a schedule that runs whether or not you are ready. Once you accept the schedule, everything else becomes easy.


Conclusion: A Long Decision, Repeated Daily

　Adopting a cat is usually described as a decision made once. In practice it is one decision repeated every morning for fifteen years — the litter box, the food, the attention, the cost. What makes it worth repeating is that a cat is honest about being small. It needs very little, it gives affection on its own terms, and it never pretends to be anything other than a warm animal that sleeps eighteen hours a day. On September 28 ZEN was the size of my two hands. Now ZEN is unmistakably a cat.
